16.0.0.en: Jehu the son of Hanani: He is the son of Hanani the seer who rebuked Asa (2 Chr 16:7) and dwelt in Jerusalem. He probably rebuked Baasha at the end of his reign, and also rebuked Jehoshaphat king of Judah for supporting the wicked King Ahab (2 Chr 19:2, 3). The prophet Jehu came before Baasha king of Israel with all boldness to rebuke him for his evil, hoping he would repent. This was at the end of Baasha's life, after he had worshiped idols and led the people astray for many years. God showed Baasha His favor to him in raising him out of the dust, for he was of the common people, and God granted him to reign over Israel. God makes clear to him that his reigning was by His permission and not by Baasha's own strength, but sadly after he became king he did not submit to God, who had given him the grace of kingship; rather he angered Him by the worship of the idols that Jeroboam had set up, and he led the people astray after him, and they provoked God and defied Him. Yet God still says "My people" despite their sins, because He is a tender and merciful Father.

16.1.0.en: The divine judgment on the sins of Baasha was to take away and destroy his offspring, as God destroyed the offspring of Jeroboam by the hand of Baasha, and their corpses would be cast out in the city, to be eaten by the dogs, and in the fields, to be eaten by the birds of prey. This is a disgrace to these kings and their offspring, because they angered God. Baasha killed the offspring of Jeroboam out of hatred for Jeroboam and not out of obedience to God; therefore God disciplines him by destroying his offspring also, just as Babylon disciplined the kingdom of Judah, but God afterward punished Babylon by means of the Medes and Persians, because it did not discipline Judah in obedience to God but out of greed and evil.

16.1.2.en: 1- The boldness of the prophet Jehu.

16.1.3.en: 2- His purpose, which was to call Baasha and his offspring to repentance.

16.1.4.en: 3- Lifting their eyes to eternity: although they would reign, they would die in a shameful manner, so that perhaps they would take heed during their reign and regain their eternity by returning to God.

16.1.5.en: 4- Reminding Baasha that the judgment that was passed on Jeroboam and his offspring, and that Baasha carried out by destroying them and treating their corpses with contempt (ch. 14:1-16), is the very same judgment passed on him, so that perhaps he would take heed and repent.

16.1.6.en: 5- God's fatherhood and tenderness toward His people, whom the wicked kings of Israel had led astray, still remain, and He calls them "My people," so that perhaps they would take heed, return to Him and leave the worship of idols.

16.1.7.en: Be attentive to what happens in your life and to the words of God that you read in the Holy Bible, for they are personal messages to you, calling you to return to God, so that you may live with Him and save yourself from many troubles on earth, and then have a place in heaven.

16.2.0.en: All the acts of Baasha are written in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel."

16.3.0.en: Tirzah: It was the center of the kingdom of the ten tribes of Israel for about fifty years. It is ten kilometers northeast of the city of Shechem, that is, Nablus.

16.3.1.en: Baasha died after a reign of twenty-four years, as mentioned in (ch. 15:23), and was buried in "Tirzah," the capital of his kingdom, and his son Elah succeeded him on the throne.

16.4.0.en: Here He confirms the punishment of God that He announced by the hand of the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani in (vv. 2, 3), as a result of the sins of Baasha and of his son Elah, who reigned after him for only two years, for the following reasons:

16.4.1.en: 1- The worship of the idols that Jeroboam set up.

16.4.2.en: 2- His violence and cruelty in killing the offspring of Jeroboam; and when this verse speaks of his killing Jeroboam, it means his killing his offspring. Although God had permitted this as a punishment for Jeroboam, Baasha did all this in order to have the kingship to himself, so that no one of the offspring of Jeroboam would oppose him, and he was very cruel in destroying them.

16.4.3.en: 3- He committed many evils, motivated by selfishness and various lusts.

16.4.4.en: For this reason God permitted the destruction of all the offspring of Baasha, exactly as Baasha did to Jeroboam; so it was done to him.

16.5.s.en: (2) Elah the son of Baasha, king of Israel

16.5.0.en: Elah succeeded his father Baasha on the throne of Israel, and this was in the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah. The capital of his kingdom was "Tirzah," and his reign was short, for he reigned only two years, and in truth he did not complete two years, because it is mentioned that Zimri, who killed him, reigned after him in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of Asa (v. 15), and part of a year is counted as a year.

16.6.0.en: Conspired: plotted and rose in revolt against him.

16.6.1.en: Zimri his servant: those who worked for the king were called his servants, whatever their positions.

16.6.2.en: One of the commanders of his army conspired against him, Zimri, captain of half his chariots. When Elah was in "Tirzah," drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, his steward who was appointed over his house, Zimri broke into the house and killed him, and this was in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and Zimri took the throne.

16.6.3.en: This shows the extent of the corruption that had spread in the kingdom of Israel: the king was occupied with his own pleasures and immersed in drinking wine, while at the same time treachery spread. So Zimri, who was trained for war, being a senior officer in the army and commander of half the chariots, attacked the king and killed him while he was drunk. Instead of the king being a leader of his army, which was fighting the Philistines (v. 15), he was absorbed in his pleasures. Perhaps the killing of King Elah was a plot agreed upon between Zimri and Arza, for there was a party among the people that followed Zimri, and perhaps Arza was one of its members, as will appear in the following verses that this party would stand against the party of Omri.

16.6.4.en: Do not be absorbed in the pleasures of the world and its evil lusts and be deceived by them, for their end is destruction. Beware of Satan, who puts poison in honey, and keep away from everything that leads you to sin and seek God, and you will delight in fellowship with Him and be always happy.

16.7.0.en: His kinsfolk: his relatives and friends and everyone who could avenge his death.

16.7.1.en: Him that pisseth against a wall: every male of his offspring.

16.7.2.en: God had sent the prophet Jehu to warn Baasha, but he paid no heed to the words of the Lord, so the time of divine punishment came, and as soon as Zimri sat on the throne he set about destroying all the relatives, friends and kinsfolk of Baasha, leaving him no relative or friend to avenge his blood, and thus the word of the Lord which He had spoken was fulfilled. The destruction of the offspring of Baasha was the natural result of his sins and of his leading astray the people of the kingdom of Israel, exactly as Jeroboam led Israel astray by the worship of idols, so God permitted the destruction of his offspring, and this shows:

16.7.3.en: 1- The cruelty and violence of Zimri in destroying the offspring of Baasha.

16.7.4.en: 2- The justice and vengeance of God: as Baasha did to the offspring of Jeroboam, so Zimri did to his offspring.

16.7.5.en: 3- The certainty that the word of God will be carried out: He is long-suffering, but His word must be fulfilled, as He announced to Baasha by the mouth of the prophet Jehu.

16.8.0.en: The rest of the acts of Elah are written in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel," which is a civil book, other than the books of Chronicles that are in the Holy Bible.

16.9.0.en: In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned in "Tirzah," but his reign lasted only one week. The army of Israel at that time was besieging "Gibbethon," which the Philistines had seized, and it seems that the dispute over Gibbethon continued for many years, for here it is mentioned that it was under siege, and also 26 years earlier, in (ch. 15:27), it was under siege in the days of Nadab the son of Jeroboam.

16.9.1.en: With the killing of Elah the second dynasty that reigned over Israel came to an end; the first dynasty was the dynasty of Jeroboam and the second was the dynasty of Baasha, and then Zimri reigned, who continued in the kingship only a few days. (See the list of the kings of Judah and Israel at the end of the book.)

16.10.0.en: The soldiers of the kingdom of Israel encamped against Gibbethon heard that Zimri had revolted against King Elah and killed him. It seems that Zimri was not loved by the whole army, so the soldiers besieging Gibbethon, who belonged to Omri, were angry at Zimri's killing of Elah, because Elah was peaceable even though he did not care for the kingdom. So they rose to avenge his blood and made Omri king over them, and they left Gibbethon and moved toward Tirzah, the capital of the kingdom, and besieged it. Tirzah was a beautiful city but unfortified, and they intended to seize Zimri and kill him after they had made Omri king, for it was in their plan to kill Zimri after enthroning Omri. Perhaps when Omri saw Zimri killing the servants and officers of King Elah, he feared for himself that Zimri would kill him, so he led the army to put an end to him.

16.11.0.en: When King Zimri saw that his capital Tirzah was under siege, since the city was unfortified and easy to storm, he was certain that Omri would seize him and even make a public spectacle of him for killing King Elah, who had preceded him. Therefore he set fire to the palace in which he dwelt, and he took his own life, and the great palace burned. Perhaps he wished that Omri should not enjoy this magnificent palace.

16.11.1.en: Thus we see that the result of the treachery and killing which Zimri committed came quickly upon his head, and he died a hard death, that is, burned in fire.

16.11.2.en: Do not be dazzled by positions and possessions so that you walk in evil to reach them. God is just, and He sees your deeds and will punish you for them, and if He is long-suffering for a time, the punishment will be harder. Be sure that evil never gives rest or happiness, but being with God and walking in His commandments is the only thing that gives you stability, assurance and happiness.

16.12.0.en: The death of Zimri in this terrible manner was a divine punishment for his sins of the worship of idols, violence and injustice, not only in his earlier life but after he became king over Israel, and by this he led the people astray and encouraged them to worship idols and do every evil. It is remarkable that this happened in only seven days, which shows that he was very wicked and began evil from the first day of his reign, so he provoked the Lord by his sins.

16.13.0.en: The details of the life of Zimri and the conspiracy that he led against Elah are written in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel."

16.14.0.en: The people were divided into two parties, one party supporting Omri, who rose against Zimri, and the other party supporting Tibni, who had backed Zimri and opposed Omri's movement and his stirring up of the army against Zimri. The division continued for four years or a little more (vv. 15, 23), from the twenty-seventh year to the thirty-first of Asa, during which civil wars arose between the two parties, in which the strength of Omri and his army appeared over the other party, which had followed Zimri and was now led by Tibni. With time this party grew weak and Tibni died, either in one of the wars or from grief at what had become of him, and by this Omri was able to reign alone over Israel, for the army was with him, and it was of course stronger than the people who supported Tibni.

16.15.0.en: In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri reigned over Israel, and his reign lasted twelve years, and "Tirzah" was the capital of his kingdom in the first six years of his reign. These six years after the death of Zimri include the four years in which the struggle with Tibni and his party was intense (vv. 21, 22), and they are in truth less than six years by some months, since they began from the twenty-seventh year of King Asa until the thirty-second.

16.16.0.en: Two talents of silver: a talent of silver has several weights, ranging between 17 and 40 kg.

16.16.1.en: Samaria: It lies north of Jerusalem at a distance of 56 km, and Omri built it in the year 924 BC, and it continued until the captivity of Israel, when the Assyrians destroyed it in the year 722 BC; its place is now the city of Sebastia. It stood on a hill and so was easy to fortify, and it was suitable as a capital.

16.16.2.en: Omri bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer, who owned it, and built on it the city of Samaria, named after Shemer, and made it the capital of his kingdom. Thus the capital moved from Shechem, which had been the seat of the kingdom, to Tirzah, and then to Samaria.

16.17.0.en: Omri surpassed all who were before him in his deviation, and that of his people, from the way of the Lord. He walked in the way of Jeroboam and led the people to pagan worship, which angered the Lord, and perhaps the evil of Omri lay in pressing the people to worship the golden calves that Jeroboam had set up, which increased the people's error.

16.18.0.en: The acts of Omri were recorded as history in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel." History declares that Omri was a politically and militarily successful leader, but sadly he was far from God by his worship of idols.

16.19.0.en: Omri died and was buried in Samaria, and his son Ahab succeeded him on the throne of Israel. Thus began the dynasty of Omri, which reigned a long time over Israel and was the most wicked of dynasties in the worship of idols and injustice (Mic 6:16).

16.19.1.en: Omri used the kingship to do evil more than all who were before him, so God punished him by destroying him and his offspring after a time. Be careful to use your abilities, your position and your circumstances to glorify God, to be joined to Him and to draw others to Him, and you will save yourself and those around you and have a place in heaven.

16.20.s.en: (5) Ahab the son of Omri, king over Israel

16.20.0.en: In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria, and his reign lasted twenty-two years.

16.21.0.en: Ahab did much evil, and the evils and sins that he committed during his reign exceeded the evils of all who sat on the throne of Israel before him and after him. Thus we find evil increasing: Omri did evil more than all who were before him, and his son Ahab learned from him and became more wicked than his father, and his pagan wife Jezebel, the daughter of the king of Sidon, helped him in that. What shows the enormity of Ahab's sins is that in his days the voice of God was clear by the mouth of the mighty Elijah, but he rejected the word of Elijah and persecuted him and tried to kill him, as will appear in the next chapter.

16.21.1.en: Beware, for the sins you commit affect your children, since you are an example. Therefore care for your relationship with God and for your repentance, and you will lead your children in the way of God.

16.22.0.en: The Zidonians: the inhabitants of Sidon, a rich coastal city famous for trade and fishing, lying in present-day Lebanon.

16.22.1.en: Ahab was not content with following the way of Jeroboam in the worship of the two golden calves, but added to that by marrying "Jezebel," the daughter of "Ethbaal" king of Sidon, and it was she who drew him to the worship of Baal, her god, and to bow down to him. He built a house for Baal in Samaria and set up an altar, which he placed in it; that is, he spread the worship of Baal and encouraged it, and the worship of the two calves that Jeroboam had set up became open pagan worship and not a symbol of the worship of God. He persecuted the prophets and the believers and killed many of them (ch. 18:4). Ahab and Jezebel became a source of evil not only in the kingdom of Israel but in Judah also, because the daughter of Ahab, Athaliah, was married to the king of Judah, and she even took the kingship alone afterward.

16.23.0.en: Ahab set up many groves for the worship of idols, so the Lord was angry with him because he increased in their worship more than all the kings of Israel who were before him.

16.24.0.en: In his days Hiel the Bethelite built Jericho. There was a curse on whoever would build the city of Jericho, spoken by the mouth of Joshua the son of Nun, and everyone knew of this curse, but the fear of God was no longer before the children of Israel, so they despised the threats of God as they had despised His promises. More than 500 years had passed since the word of the Lord by the mouth of Joshua, but the Lord had not forgotten His word, so Abiram the firstborn son of Hiel died when he laid the foundations of the city, and his youngest son Segub died when he set up its gates, and probably the rest of his sons died afterward. Jericho had already been built as dwellings, as mentioned in (Josh 16:1, 7, 18:12), but what is meant here is its being built as a fortified city.

16.24.1.en: Elijah, the famine and the raising of the widow's son
